summary: Explains the idea of a network transport circuit breaker, why tunnels and applications using non-congestion-controlled traffic need them, and what requirements one must meet. It is a BCP.

eli5.summary: A safety switch that shuts off traffic that ignores traffic jams, to protect everyone.

subtitle: A last-resort safety switch that cuts off traffic causing persistent, excessive congestion when nothing else slows it down.

tldr.problem: Traffic that does not use congestion control, such as many UDP applications and tunnels, can persistently overload a link and starve other flows.
tldr.mechanism: A network transport circuit breaker meters traffic at an ingress and an egress, compares the two over a long timescale, and when persistent excessive congestion is seen it terminates or sharply reduces the traffic.
tldr.outcome: The RFC says where circuit breakers are recommended, gives 17 design requirements, and shows Fast-Trip, Slow-Trip and Managed examples.

facts.label: Minimum reduction (SHOULD)
facts.value: At least an order of magnitude

facts.label: SAToP example
facts.value: 1 second period, more than three SES

today: RFC 8084 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 208), and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the published guidance on when circuit breakers are needed and how to design them.

sections.title: What a Network Circuit Breaker Is
sections.content:
The name comes from electricity supply, not from network circuits. An electrical circuit breaker (CB) is a protection mechanism of last resort that should not trigger in normal use. A network transport circuit breaker plays the same role: an automatic mechanism that continuously monitors a flow or an aggregate of flows, looks for persistent excessive congestion, and then terminates or significantly reduces the flow(s).

The need grew from history. Persistent congestion in the 1980s Internet was countered by congestion control in TCP. Today non-congestion-controlled traffic, including many UDP applications, can be a significant share of a link, so the way it is forwarded needs thought.

CBs are recommended for IETF protocols and tunnels that carry non-congestion-controlled flows and for traffic aggregates. Application developers are advised to use proper congestion control where possible, since an application that does will be aware of congestion and is expected to avoid triggering a CB.
sections.eli5: Some traffic ignores traffic jams and keeps pushing. The circuit breaker is the emergency switch that finally stops it.

sections.title: How a CB Differs from Congestion Control
sections.content:
Congestion control in TCP, SCTP and DCCP works on the timescale of a packet round-trip time (RTT), adapting the sending rate continuously, usually per flow. Congestion can be signalled by loss or by ECN Congestion Experienced marks (RFC 3168).

A CB works on much longer timescales, from seconds to possibly many tens of seconds, and only reacts to abnormal congestion. The long period gives congestion control time to adjust and the load time to stabilize, so a single event, or even several, does not trip it. Examples of triggering conditions include anomalous traffic above provisioned capacity, routing changes that add traffic to a monitored path, and misconfigured devices, admission controllers or policers.

Other operational tools may react faster. The CB stays the method of last resort and should trigger only when those did not succeed.

The RFC names three kinds, mainly by trigger timescale: Fast-Trip (protects a single flow or related group), Slow-Trip (protects against traffic aggregates) and Managed (uses operations and management functions).
sections.eli5: Normal traffic rules react in a blink. The circuit breaker waits and only acts when the jam clearly will not clear up by itself.

sections.title: Functional Components of a CB
sections.content:
A CB involves an ingress point (the sender or tunnel entrance) and an egress point (the receiver or tunnel exit), which can be network devices or transport endpoints. The RFC lists seven components:

  1. An ingress meter counting packets or bytes sent per measurement interval, which measures the offered load.
  2. An egress meter counting what is received, the supported load. It may also use loss or congestion marking.
  3. A way to carry both measurements to the measurement function: return packets, OAM, in-band datagrams or an SDN controller.
  4. A measurement function that combines them, for example deducing loss from the difference between counters. High accuracy is not needed, because isolated or infrequent loss is to be disregarded.
  5. A trigger function that compares against a threshold, preferably a rate or ratio such as more than 10% loss, in multiple intervals such as three successive measurements.
  6. A reaction at the ingress that removes the offending traffic.
  7. A feedback control that triggers when measurements are not available, since lost control packets can also signal heavy congestion.

The same ideas apply to other topologies. With multicast, an egress endpoint that sees excessive loss sends a leave message (IGMP or MLD), and the multicast control plane prunes traffic, so the CB controls only traffic downstream of the first-hop router. CBs can also run alongside control protocols for pre-provisioned capacity, and can control unidirectional UDP traffic if a control-message path exists.
sections.eli5: One meter counts what goes in, another counts what comes out, and a judge notices if too much goes missing for too long and flips the switch.

sections.title: Requirements for a CB
sections.content:
Section 4 lists 17 numbered requirements. The main themes are:

  • Robust measurement. A CB MUST define a measurement period, longer than the time congestion control needs to react, and MUST know that packets were lost or marked. ECN CE marks may be counted, but loss MUST also be measured.
  • No false alarms. A CB MUST NOT trigger under light or intermittent congestion. It MUST define a threshold and a triggering interval, long enough not to penalize flows with long path RTTs, and MUST be robust to multiple congestion events.
  • A severe reaction. The normal reaction SHOULD disable all traffic that contributed. If it only reduces traffic, the reduction SHOULD be at least an order of magnitude, and the CB MUST keep monitoring and react again if triggered again. The reaction MUST last at least the triggering interval, and automated reset MUST NOT be immediate or happen with evidence of continued congestion.
  • Logging. A trigger SHOULD be treated as an abnormal event and logged, with the measurements behind it.
  • Control messages. They MUST be robust to loss, without needing reliable delivery such as TCP. In-band control is RECOMMENDED. In-band designs SHOULD treat repeated loss of control messages as a sign of congestion, while out-of-band designs SHOULD NOT trigger on lost measurements. Shared-path control traffic is RECOMMENDED to be prioritized.
  • Protection. Authenticity and integrity of control messages MUST be protected from off-path attacks, and cryptographic authentication is RECOMMENDED when on-path attacks are a risk.
sections.eli5: A good fuse must not pop on a small flicker, must really cut the power when it does pop, and must not be easy for a prankster to trigger.

sections.title: Examples of CBs
sections.content:
A Fast-Trip CB is the most responsive form, with a response time only slightly larger than the traffic it controls. It suits traffic with well-understood characteristics and could trigger prematurely on aggregates. For RTP, a set of Fast-Trip methods (RFC 8083) uses in-band RTCP reports and shuts the flow down when, for example, no receiver reports arrive, progress is not reported, long-term throughput exceeds a TFRC-like hard limit, or media quality falls below a minimum.

A Slow-Trip CB responds much more slowly and is expected to be more common. A typical need is a tunnel in the general Internet whose inner flows do not all use TCP-style congestion control.

A Managed CB lives in the signaling protocol or management plane and suits controlled environments. For SAToP pseudowires (RFC 4553), the recommended measurement period is 1 second and the trigger fires on more than three Severely Errored Seconds, after which the pseudowire shuts down for some time. RFC 7893 suggests the same approach for inelastic TDM pseudowires, and an operator response gives a chance to restore service quality.
sections.eli5: There are quick switches for traffic you understand well, slow ones for big mixed crowds, and ones run by a human operator.

sections.title: When a CB May Not Be Needed
sections.content:
A CB is not required for a single congestion-controlled flow using TCP, SCTP, TFRC and similar, since their congestion control already prevents persistent excessive congestion.

Three cases are discussed. With pre-provisioned capacity, compliant traffic should not cause persistent congestion, so a CB triggers only on noncompliant traffic. Adding one does not reduce performance and protects others if traffic is rerouted onto an unprovisioned path. For tunnels carrying congestion-controlled traffic, a CB can still help: an aggregate of many short flows may end before reacting, and a provider often cannot know the tunnel holds only congestion-controlled traffic. If the aggregate causes no persistent excessive congestion, the CB simply does not trigger. A one-way path with no control path cannot be controlled by a CB; mitigation is ingress policing and operator monitoring.
sections.eli5: If a car already has its own brakes and the road is private, a fuse may not be needed, but having one does no harm.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Every CB relies on control information moving across the network, so that information is an attack target. An attacker who injects fake or modified measurements, for example claiming high loss, could make a CB trigger and so mount a denial-of-service attack on the controlled traffic.

The RFC says authenticity and integrity of control messages MUST be protected from off-path attacks. Simple protection is a randomized source port or similar header fields such as the RTP SSRC and sequence number. Stronger protection comes from a secure authentication protocol, and cryptographic authentication of all control messages is RECOMMENDED, with a stated trade-off against its cost.

The measurement period matters too: too long and the CB responds slowly, too short and it may trigger prematurely. Control traffic uses capacity, so it should be considered in design and provisioning. Each CB design MUST evaluate whether it has new security implications.
sections.eli5: If a prankster could fake a message saying the road is jammed, they could make the switch pop for no reason, so the messages must be protected.
